BLOGBY STEPHANIE MOSS, MD

Considerations Before Taking a Leave of Absence (LOA) from Medical School

Survey Responses & Advice LOA & Residency Application In this post I have consolidated all the information on taking a Leave of Absence (LOA) from Medical School and how to discuss it in your residency application. The below information comes from my own experience taking an LOA between my 2nd and 3rd year of medical school, and the results of multiple surveys of medical students who have similarly taken an LOA. The first survey (17 respondents) which found that 53% of respondents stated they were not given information from their school on important things to consider. Therefore, this article is written to meet this highly requested need. If you would like to share your experience fill out this anonymous survey created with collaboration with Tufts Medical School. Poster on LOA Presented at the 2025 American Psychiatric Association Meeting The school usually requires or "highly recommends" a LOA Usually because one has failed too many courses, has to retake a year, or has to retake a board exam. This is seen not as favorably by residencies (confirmed by multiple Program Directors and Advisors) 53% of survey respondents Can be for ANY reason (see below) Usually considered a "choice" to take a leave One does not need to explain WHY to their school 35% of survey respondents Do have to provide an explanation in the Residency Application Process (see below) ***When one takes a LOA from medical school, one must sign a piece of paper from administration check marking one of these two options Here are some reasons students have reported taking a LOA in the survey, individual interviews, and through online research Study for USMLE STEP: 59% of respondents Necessitate a greater time for dedicated STEP studying than the school's allotted time frame Step1: usually 2 months provided for dedicatedStep2: usually 2 - 8 weeks available as Elective time during M4 year Step1: usually 2 months provided for dedicated Step2: usually 2 - 8 weeks available as Elective time during M4 year Time to request disability accommodations Need to retake the exam after a failure Personal health - 41% of respondents Acute mental health condition Chronic mental health condition Acute physical health condition Chronic physical health condition Burnout - 35% of respondents Family obligations- 24% of respondents Acute Illness or Disability Professional - 12% of respondents Special or unique opportunity in dream job/position Unable to qualify for student loans nor have an endorser Work to financially support self, family, or partner Personal Time - 6% of respondents Enjoy life outside of school Of respondents 41% took an LOA between 2nd and 3rd year and 29.4% took an LOA between their 3rd and 4th year of medical school. Considerations before taking an LOA: How will you finance the months or year off? This is the #1 concern, fear, and challenge of students taking a LOA Funding options included personal savings, work, family support, and public financial aid assistance programs. Food stamps (SNAP) Application if you have NO family financial support or external income is under $0 State or city utilities Support WIC: If you or your partner is pregnant or have a young child How will you finance Health Insurance? Do you have a partner that you can go on their plan? Some schools allow you to remain on the same plan but you will need to pay out of pocket. For example mine cost $4,000 for 9 months off of school For example mine cost $4,000 for 9 months off of school Are you eligible for Medicaid? Most residency's recommend and provide disability insurance to residents because one never knows when a visible or invisible disability can arise which could impair you temporarily from working However, rarely do medical schools recommend, provide, or encourage students to get disability insurance The AAMC mandates medical schools have disability insurance available as a benefit to students but this is not advertised to students Most plans provide: $1,500/month to 1st & 2nd year medical students on LOA$2,000/month to 2nd & 3rd year medical students on LOA $1,500/month to 1st & 2nd year medical students on LOA $2,000/month to 2nd & 3rd year medical students on LOA See an example of the benefit at Loyola Medical School in Chicago Do you need to move back home or with a family member?Multiple students reported needing to give up their lease or housing to move in with family because they did not have the student loans to pay for rentSome students had to travel multiple states and pay out of pocket for travel and moving expenses Multiple students reported needing to give up their lease or housing to move in with family because they did not have the student loans to pay for rent Some students had to travel multiple states and pay out of pocket for travel and moving expenses Check eligibility for Affordable Housing and Grants Some students struggled so much with affording housing that they were at risk of being evicted for being late on making rent payments Does your school provide you continued access to academic study spaces and tutoring services? Here are my suggestions on how to study for STEP1 and Not Fail 59% of students studied for STEP1 or STEP2 during their LOAPreparing for STEP is expensive because you have to pay for each practice test and practice questions (UWorld) which can be around $500 totalEvery time one re-schedulees the STEP exam there is a $100-200 fee Preparing for STEP is expensive because you have to pay for each practice test and practice questions (UWorld) which can be around $500 total Every time one re-schedulees the STEP exam there is a $100-200 fee 19% of students paid for a private tutoring service 13% of students received tutoring through their school Are there any current or previous students at your school who took an LOA who can provide you advice or mentorship? We created GroupMe for Medical Students in our school which included around 30 students who have been on or are currently on an LOA which has been helpful to remind ourselves that "You are NOT ALONE" Does your health insurance or school cover therapy and counselling services? Study Results:60% of respondents said they felt alone or very alone during their LOA 60% of respondents said they felt alone or very alone during their LOA 56% of respondents responded “Not at all” (1) vs 0% responded "very emotionally supported" (5) to the school providing emotional support during their LOA The "Choice" of Taking an LOA Survey Responses & Advice: I sent out a survey to my student group of ~30 students who have taken an LOA at my school in the past 4 years. I also advertised the survey to the current M2,M3, M4, and Interns in case anyone took an LOA and I didn't know about. I also sent the survey out to a couple medical students which I had met at conferences and social media who had taken an LOA from medical school. Final Results: from 17 students who responded Question: What fears did you have about taking an LOA? "Financial. Also I am incredibly close to my classmates and I was afraid I wouldn’t graduate without their support." "Possible red flag on application to residency." "Impact on matching into residency and lack of financial support" "Financial and if I could achieve academically" "How I would pay for housing, food, and health care with out my student loans" "Negative impact on residency applications" Question: What fears do you have after taking an LOA? "Applying to residency programs and talking about my LOA-this is still an issue." "Impact on matching into residency" "Step 1 and residency apps" "Being able to match into residency because of the LOA red flag" "Same reasons, but also that I started to feel a little indifference and freedom being out of the medical field" Question: What are some things you wish you knew before taking LOA? "You will feel behind since your class will be 'ahead'" "How alone I would feel. The stigma around it." "Financial aid changes and having to pay back to the school for loans I had already taken out and used" "More information on how an LOA would impact my future career, especially the perception of an LOA by residency program directors" "Understanding how to navigate the financial issues with discontinued loans" "I unfortunately was caught in more financial struggle than I imagined and my school was going through a curriculum change that has made me have to start third year later than I thought" On the 2023 Residency Application this box was included: "Was your medical education/training extended or interrupted?" (510-characters) Since it is only 510 characters you have to be "short and sweet" Make sure to state facts and are honest Make sure to include 1-2 sentences of what one learned and how the experience was meaningful to their future career as a physician One can always include more in their personal statement, activities, and box for "Impactful Experiences" 750 character limit (with spaces) I was told by a Residency Director that they can filter by students who have had NO MORE than 4 years of medical school, this means that an individual who has taken an LOA (an extra year of medical school) would be filtered out Out of the 44 programs I applied I have received ~20 interviews even though I have taken an LOA. However, I did receive rejections and haven't received replies from residency programs that might have filtered me out for my LOA Rarely have I been out-right asked about my LOA, but I have been asked about the topics sounding my LOA experience since it was a significant time point in my medical journey (health, financially, professionally, and academically). Specialties offering interviews to respondents who have taken LOA include Psychiatry, Family Medicine, and Neurology Demonstrate to programs lessons learned and how the experience provided you skills that will make you a better physician such as resiliency, perseverance, and adaptability.
